cells.tense: The practice is carrying itself at the moment, and setting it down would not cost you what it built.
cells.act: let one structure collapse that could not hold
cells.ask: Find a piece of your routine that only runs on pressure — the extra set, the drill you dread but keep. Leave it out and watch what still works without it.
cells.core:
You can tell what the work needs from what you've added to feel safe. The steady hour still happens, the repetitions still stack, and you set something down without the whole thing falling. What you refine gets better rather than smaller, and the quiet is company rather than a room you've locked.

Too much of this is propped up by effort. The drill you've outgrown, the part of the routine that exists because of an old fear — stop holding it up. It comes down under its own weight. Clear the ground it leaves and leave the ground clear. What belongs back will earn its place.
cells.sheetLine: You can drop what only holds by force.
cells.verb: keep a small light lit by attending to it — practice, refined through repetition
cells.place: the quiet hour where the same act is done again, alone, until it becomes skill

cells.tense: The next session is already being rehearsed against a standard you won't be able to meet twice.
cells.act: release it on purpose, not by losing it
cells.ask: Name the outcome you grip hardest — how a session should go, a number you chase. Put it down for one round, deliberately, and let your hands stay idle while it happens.
cells.core:
The practice has stopped being the thing and become the standard it has to meet. You refine past the point where refining helps, and the next session is already judged before it starts. Sitting with it alone reads as a requirement rather than a choice, and the fear when you stop tells you how tight the grip has been. You're not lazy — you're braced.

Loosen one hand. Choose the outcome you grip hardest — how a session should go, a number you're after — and release it deliberately, once. Not by failing at it; on purpose. Let the round happen without the verdict attached. What's underneath the grip is the practice you actually love, and it's still there.

cells.tense: The steady hour has stood shut for a while, and you can see it clearly from outside without sitting in it.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: Take a practice you keep meaning to begin and a habit that owns the same hour. Give the practice that hour once, then stop there whatever happened.
cells.core:
What you can do in one burst doesn't carry into the next, so the same act gets rehearsed in your head and rarely done. The years of almost doing it stack up as something you nearly had. You can see the hour from outside and not sit in it.

Start with a trade rather than a discipline. Find an hour that a habit currently owns and give it to the practice — once, and no more than once — then stop. Adjust the share until it's fair, and stop when it is. If the week passes and you didn't go, change the share and try once more. This doesn't ask you to be someone else.

cells.tense: You've been getting good at this without ever having decided to, and the hours where it happened don't count in your story.
cells.act: picture it a year on, turned out well, and keep the picture
cells.ask: Picture this practice a year ahead, going the way you'd want. Set that on one page — whatever you can see of it — and keep the page where you'll meet it.
cells.core:
The skill is already there: you do the thing well, you've done it well for a long time, and you'd tell anyone you're not really practicing. The hours went somewhere. You either can't see the hand that did the work or you'd rather not claim it, so it arrives as talent or luck or just how you are. The practice keeps running in the background, unattended, while you stand outside it.

Imagine this a year ahead, going the way you'd want it to. Name the work, the person you'd be by then, and set the picture down on a page you keep. You're not swearing to anything — just letting the version you already want stand visible somewhere. The next step only needs that much light.
cells.sheetLine: You've been practicing. The hours went somewhere.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is in the Too Little cell: the record says past experience made practice feel dangerous, but it does not say what happened, who was involved, or when — I locate the person behind the present without narrating the past. A reader could reasonably say 'it's not fear, I've just never had a reason to build one.' The ask survives being wrong: adjusting one exchange between one thing you put in and one thing you get back is useful, harmless, and teaches something even if the diagnosis is off. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line about 'protecting yourself from practice' — I've cut that. The Too Much read could land as blame for loving the work; the read describes tempo and grip, not the person's character, and the ask is a held breath, not a renunciation.
